fatal_errors: The cited evidence does not address AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, nanoscale surface segregation, in situ heating, or the proposed Au/Cu evaporation mechanism.

The attribution of Au/Cu loss primarily to their relatively low boiling points is unsupported and oversimplifies the target mechanism, which involves surface-energy-driven segregation followed by shell melting and evaporation near 973 K.
The proposed 600–800 K threshold is too broad to recover the reported onset near 673 K.
explanation: The hypothesis captures the central reconstruction: diffusion is not sluggish, nanoscale surface-energy differences drive Au and Cu enrichment, and heating produces loss of small particles, distribution broadening, and spherical reshaping. It also recognizes the sub-10 nm and morphology-dependent boundary and proposes a reasonably discriminating combination of in situ STEM and atomistic simulation. However, the intervention omits the 298–973 K ramp at 1 K/s, discrete temperature steps, vacuum-only condition, and analysis-time constraint. It also fails to specify the reported Au/Cu shell melting and evaporation at 973 K or the approximately 22% size reduction. The statement that configurational entropy stabilizes the bulk FCC structure sits uneasily with the target conclusion that the observed structure is predominantly kinetically governed. The experiment would be stronger with simultaneous STEM-EDS measurements of surface Au/Cu concentration, explicit Au self-diffusivity extraction, and matched icosahedral versus truncated-octahedral particles. Most importantly, none of E1–E3 provides relevant support, so the evidence discipline is inadequate despite substantial mechanistic agreement.
